## Slide 1

Lenz's Law, Pulling a Wire.

Pulling a wire through a magnetic field induces an EMF and a current in the circuit it completes.

Our big question for this lesson: how do transformers help distribute electricity across the power grid? First, we need one more rule about induction. Imagine your hand is pulling the wire through the magnetic field in Figure 9. As you pull, the wire's motion induces an EMF. The wire slides along a wire loop, completing a circuit, so the EMF drives a current.

The magnetic field B points out of the page and the velocity points to the right. The right-hand rule shows the current in the wire is downward, which makes it flow clockwise around the circuit.

## Slide 3

Opposing Motion.

The force on an induced current opposes the motion that produced it.

Now the charges moving down the wire are themselves moving through a field that points out of the page, so they feel a force too. The right-hand rule shows this force points opposite to the way you're pulling the wire. Those charges push back on the wire, opposing its motion and making it harder to pull.

The physicist H. F. E. Lenz first demonstrated this force in 1834. It's the universe making sure you pay, in work, for the electrical energy you get.

## Slide 4

Opposing Change.

Lenz's law: the magnetic field produced by an induced current opposes the change in the original field.

Lenz described his law in terms of force, but there's a second way to see it. The induced current makes its own magnetic field. Inside the loop in Figure 9, that field points into the paper, opposing the change that caused it. So Lenz's law says the magnetic field produced by an induced current always opposes the change in the original field.

Look at the coil in Figure 10. The approaching magnet increases the field inside the coil, so the induced current flows counterclockwise, making a field that opposes the increase. That induced field repels the magnet, and by Newton's third law, the magnet pushes the coil away. Pull the magnet away, and the field in the coil decreases, so now the induced current flows clockwise, making a field that adds to the magnet's field.

Either way, the induced field fights the change. Flip the magnet so its south pole faces the coil, and the current reverses, but the force on the coil still pushes it away as the magnet approaches.

## Slide 5

Lenz's Law in Generators.

A generator supplying current is harder to turn because the induced current's field opposes the armature's motion.

Lenz's law shapes how generators and motors work. When a generator isn't connected to a circuit, turning its armature induces an EMF but no current. No current means no magnetic field from it, so there's no opposing force, and the armature is easy to turn.

Connect it to a circuit, though, and the induced EMF drives a current. That current's magnetic field pushes on the armature, opposite to the force you're using to turn it, so it gets hard to turn. A generator supplying a large current produces lots of electrical energy, and it takes a correspondingly larger amount of mechanical energy to keep it going. That's conservation of energy in action.

## Slide 6

Lenz's Law in Motors.

A spinning motor induces an EMF that opposes its current, so a loaded or stalled motor draws more current.

When you first switch on a motor, like a vacuum cleaner, the current is large. As soon as the motor starts turning, its wires cut through the magnetic field and induce an EMF that opposes the current. So the current drops.

Now put a load on the motor, like lifting a weight. The motor slows down, which shrinks the opposing EMF, so the current goes up. More current means electrical energy flows into the motor faster, and that energy goes out as mechanical work on the load, just as conservation of energy demands. If the load is big enough to stop the motor, the current can get so high that the wires overheat.

## Slide 7

Dimming Lights and Sparking Switches.

A starting motor's large current lowers the voltage for other devices, and switching a motor off can induce a spark.

Ever notice your lights dim when the air conditioner, a table saw, or another motor kicks on? A starting motor draws a big current. The wires between the motor and its source have some resistance, so that big current increases the potential difference across the wires. A lightbulb in parallel with the motor is left with less, so it dims.

And why do switches sometimes spark? When you switch off a motor or pull its plug, the magnetic field in the motor collapses to zero. Any change in the field around a wire induces an EMF that opposes the change. That induced EMF can be big enough to make a spark jump across the switch, or between the plug and the outlet.

## Slide 8

Braking Effect and Eddy Currents.

Eddy currents are currents generated in any piece of metal moving through a magnetic field, and their field opposes the motion.

Lenz's law can be really useful. A laboratory balance uses induced currents to stop its swinging when you put something on the pan. A piece of metal on the balance arm sits between the poles of a horseshoe magnet, as in Figure 11. When the arm swings, the metal moves through the field, and the induced EMF drives swirling currents in the metal, called eddy currents, that slow it down.

Eddy currents form in any piece of metal moving through a magnetic field, and their field opposes the motion. The force works against motion in either direction, but disappears when the metal is still, so it doesn't change the mass reading.

When eddy currents slow down metal, it's called eddy-current damping. Some trains and roller coasters use it in their brakes. Sometimes it's unwanted, though. To cut down eddy currents in motors, their cores are built from thin metal layers with insulation between them.

## Slide 9

Levitation.

An induced current's opposing field can repel a conductor strongly enough to make it levitate.

Lenz's law can even make things float! In Figure 12, AC current in a coil makes a changing magnetic field that induces an EMF in both aluminum rings above it. In the uncut top ring, the EMF drives a current whose field opposes the change in the coil's field. Like poles face each other, so the coil and the ring repel, and the ring rises.

The lower ring doesn't rise. It's been sawed through, so it's an incomplete circuit, and no current flows. No current, no force, no levitation. If the rings were made of a nonconductor like nylon or wood, no current would flow in either one.

Repulsion like this is behind magnetic levitation, or Maglev, trains. As they speed along, they never touch the track.

## Slide 10

Self-Inductance.

Self-inductance is the property of a wire to create an induced EMF that opposes changes in the current through it.

An EMF can be induced whenever the magnetic field around a wire changes. That field can come from outside, or from the wire's own current, as in Figure 13.

Suddenly connect the coil to a battery. The current starts to change, which changes the coil's magnetic field, which induces an EMF opposing the change. So at first the current is small, rising more slowly than it would without the coil. As the current's rate of change shrinks, so does the opposing EMF. When the current reaches its steady final value, it's no longer changing, so the induced EMF is zero.

If the battery's voltage drops, the current starts to drop, and now the induced EMF pushes in the same direction as the battery's current, trying to keep the field up. Disconnect the coil suddenly, and the induced EMF can be big enough to make a spark. This tendency of a wire, straight or coiled, to induce an EMF opposing changes in its current is called self-inductance.

## Slide 11

Transformers.

Transformers are devices that increase or decrease potential differences with relatively little waste of energy.

You've probably seen metal cylinders mounted on utility poles, like those in Figure 14. Inside each one is a transformer. Transformers raise or lower potential differences with relatively little wasted energy. These ones lower high voltages to usable levels before electrical energy enters your home.

Only alternating current can be sent through a transformer. Direct current can't pass through one, and you're about to see why.

## Slide 12

How Transformers Work.

Mutual inductance is an EMF and current induced in one coil by a changing current in another coil.

Self-inductance happens in a single coil. A transformer has two coils, insulated from each other but wound around the same iron core, as in Figure 15. Connect the first coil, the primary coil, to an AC source. Its changing current creates a changing magnetic field, which the core carries over to the second coil, the secondary coil.

In the secondary coil, that changing field induces a varying EMF and current. An EMF and current in one coil caused by a changing current in another coil is called mutual inductance. With DC, the field wouldn't change, so nothing would be induced in the secondary coil. That's why transformers need AC.

## Slide 13

Step-Up and Step-Down Transformers.

The ratio of primary to secondary potential difference equals the ratio of primary to secondary turns, V p over V s equals N p over N s.

The EMF in the secondary coil, called the secondary potential difference, is proportional to the potential difference supplied to the primary coil. It also depends on the turns ratio, the number of turns in the secondary coil divided by the number in the primary. In equation form, V p over V s equals N p over N s.

If the secondary potential difference is bigger than the primary, as on the left of Figure 15, it's a step-up transformer. For example, 5 primary turns and 20 secondary turns turn 100 volts into 400 volts. If the secondary potential difference is smaller, as on the right, it's a step-down transformer. For example, 50 primary turns and 10 secondary turns turn 100 volts into 20 volts.

So the difference comes down to the turns: a step-up transformer has more turns on its secondary coil, and a step-down transformer has fewer.

## Slide 14

The Ideal Transformer.

The transformer equation: I s over I p equals V p over V s equals N p over N s.

In an ideal transformer, the power delivered to the secondary circuit equals the power supplied to the primary circuit. It wastes nothing, 100 percent efficient. So P p equals P s, or V p times I p equals V s times I s. Rearranged, this shows the primary current depends on how much current the secondary circuit needs.

Combine that with the turns relationship, and you get the transformer equation: I s over I p equals V p over V s, which also equals N p over N s.

Here's the pattern. In a step-up transformer, V p is less than V s, I p is greater than I s, and N p is less than N s. In a step-down transformer, it's all flipped: V p is greater than V s, I p is less than I s, and N p is greater than N s. In the step-up example, 100 volts at 10 amperes becomes 400 volts at 2.5 amperes, and both sides carry 1000 watts.

## Slide 15

Real and Isolation Transformers.

A transformer's efficiency is the ratio of its output power to its input power, typically 95 to 98 percent.

Since a transformer can't create power, a step-up transformer that raises the voltage must supply less current to the secondary circuit. And a step-down transformer supplies more current than it draws. That's true even for real transformers, which aren't 100 percent efficient.

Not every transformer steps up or down. In an isolation transformer, both coils have the same number of turns, so the output voltage matches the input. These are used for safety: they electrically separate sensitive devices from the supply, blocking any DC and stray ground paths that could cause interference or shocks. Computers, recording equipment, and medical tools like ultrasound machines use them, and they can also cut electrical noise.

Ideal transformers turn no electrical energy into thermal energy, but real ones do, warming the transformer and the air around it. That reduces the power the secondary circuit can deliver. Efficiency is output power divided by input power, and typical transformers are 95 to 98 percent efficient. That loss may sound small, but big transformers handle so much power that they can get very hot.

## Slide 16

Example Problem 2, Step-Up Transformers.

V s equals N s V p over N p, and for an ideal transformer, I p equals V s I s over V p.

A step-up transformer has 200 turns on its primary coil and 3000 turns on its secondary coil. The primary coil gets an effective AC potential difference of 90.0 volts. What's the potential difference in the secondary circuit? And if the secondary current is 2.0 amperes, what's the primary current?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Draw an iron core with turns of wire on each side, and label I, V, and N. Known: N p is 200, N s is 3000, V p is 90.0 volts, and I s is 2.0 amperes. Unknown: V s and I p.

Step two: solve. V s over V p equals N s over N p, so V s equals N s times V p divided by N p. That's 3000 times 90.0 volts divided by 200, or 1350 volts. For the current, assume 100 percent efficiency, so primary and secondary power are equal: V p times I p equals V s times I s. Solve for I p: 1350 volts times 2.0 amperes, divided by 90.0 volts, is 3.0 times ten to the first amperes, or 30 amperes.

Step three: evaluate. Potential difference is in volts and current in amperes. A big step-up turns ratio gives a big secondary voltage and a smaller secondary current, and that's what we got.

## Slide 17

Everyday Uses of Transformers.

Step-up transformers raise voltages for long-distance transmission, and step-down transformers lower them for homes and devices.

Sending electrical energy long distances is only economical at very high potential differences. High voltage means less current in the transmission lines, which keeps wasted energy low. That's exactly why AC won the war of the currents: transformers make it easy to raise and lower AC voltages.

Follow the path in Figure 16. Wind spins a turbine, turning an armature in a magnetic field and inducing an EMF. At a substation, step-up transformers raise the voltage, to hundreds of thousands of volts, such as 480,000 volts. Near homes, step-down transformers bring it down to 120 volts.

Game systems, printers, laptops, and rechargeable toys have even smaller transformers inside their cases or in blocks on their cords. These lower the wall-outlet voltage further, to somewhere between 3 and 26 volts.
